stories.title: Azora, Vizcaya Capital Flip Coconut Grove Office Building for $62M
stories.excerpt: Just a year after buying a boutique office building in Miami’s coveted Coconut Grove neighborhood, Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold it for a nearly $15 million gain. The five-story property at 3250 Mary Street, called the Grove at 3250 Mary, sold for $62.3 million, according to the brokers who represented the sellers, Berkadia’s Omar Morales and Jaret Turkell. The joint venture had purchased the 80,000-square-foot building for $47.5 million last September. Records show the buyer is an entity tied to El-Ad National Properties, the Boca Raton-based division of Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva’s El-Ad Group. “Coconut Grove continues to distinguish itself as one of South Florida’s strongest real estate markets, driven by exceptional demand from luxury residential buyers and high-net-worth office users,” Morales said in a statement. “That demand, combined with limited supply, continues to attract remarkable investment to the neighborhood.” In recent years, Coconut Grove has attracted a slew of billionaires, including Google’s billionaire founder Larry Page, who spent about $170 million assembling a residential compound last year. The residential acquisitions have fueled demand for luxury office space nearby. The acquisition of the 1982-built, 1.3-acre site office building marks somewhat of a deviation for El-Ad National, which has typically focused on residential and mixed-use development. It also comes just four months after the developer purchased a nearby, low-rise condo building for $45.5 million, which will likely be redeveloped. Earlier this month, up north in Fort Lauderdale, the firm bought an oceanfront hotel for $60 million. A representative for El-Ad Group was not immediately available for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialoserver.com.
bullets: Azora/Vizcaya flipped Coconut Grove office building for $62.3M, up $14.8M in one year.
Israeli billionaire El-Ad Group acquired five-story, 80K SF asset at 3250 Mary Street.
Coconut Grove office demand driven by luxury residential spillover and high-net-worth tenants.
stories.summary: Azora Private Solutions and Vizcaya Capital sold a 80,000-square-foot office building in Miami's Coconut Grove for $62.3 million, just one year after acquiring it for $47.5 million. El-Ad National Properties (Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva's firm) purchased the property. The rapid appreciation reflects strong investor demand in Coconut Grove, fueled by luxury residential growth and affluent office users seeking limited supply.
stories.impact: Office-to-residential conversion interest in Coconut Grove remains speculative, but the $15M gain in 12 months signals robust capital competition in the submarket. This inflates land and development costs for new multifamily projects in South Florida's highest-demand neighborhoods, tightening feasibility for ground-up residential development absent significant rent growth or density upside.

stories.title: NAR: Utah City Ranks Highest in U.S. for Commercial Real Estate Demand
stories.excerpt: St. George, UT ranks as the No.1 overall metro area for demand, according to the National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) inaugural Commercial Real Estate (CRE) Demand Index. The Utah city posted an overall score of 128, with multifamily as the strongest driver. The newly introduced quarterly index of 306 U.S. metro areas measures where demand is building across office, industrial, retail and multifamily sectors. Rather than measuring current property-market conditions such as vacancy rates, rents or leasing activity, the index focuses on local economic conditions that can generate demand for commercial space and provides an early view of market trends before they are reflected in traditional commercial real estate indicators such as leasing activity and vacancy rates, according to NAR. “Commercial real estate demand begins with what’s happening in the local economy,” said Nadia Evangelou, principal economist & director of real estate research at NAR. “Demand starts before a lease is signed. It starts with jobs and people. The CRE Demand Index helps identify those trends earlier, before they’re reflected in traditional market indicators.” According to the index, South Carolina ranks as the nation’s strongest state for CRE demand, reflecting continued momentum across the Carolinas. Accordingly, Raleigh, NC ranks highest among the 50 largest metro areas with a score of 121. The post NAR: Utah City Ranks Highest in U.S. for Commercial Real Estate Demand appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: St. George, UT ranks No. 1 nationally on NAR's new CRE Demand Index with score of 128.
Multifamily is strongest demand driver in St. George; South Carolina also ranks top nationally.
Index measures local economic conditions (jobs, population) preceding traditional lease/vacancy metrics.
stories.summary: The National Association of Realtors introduced a Commercial Real Estate Demand Index tracking 306 U.S. metros across four sectors. St. George, Utah posted the highest overall score (128), with multifamily as its primary demand engine. The index prioritizes underlying economic drivers—job creation, population growth—over lagging indicators like vacancy rates and rents, providing early signals of market strength.
stories.impact: St. George's top ranking signals explosive demographic and job growth ahead of rent compression; developers should prioritize land acquisition and permitting in Utah's Wasatch Front now, before multifamily fundamentals tighten and land costs spike. The index itself validates leading-indicator discipline and may shift investor capital toward growing metros before traditional metrics warm, compressing development windows and cost advantages.

stories.title: W. Valley Data Center Developer Building Massive Energy System
stories.excerpt: For data centers to make their way through the permitting process, the developer most likely will have to provide power for the project without taxing current delivery systems. Copia Power is promoting a plan to do just that in Tonopah, a town about an hour west of Phoenix. The Phoenix Business Journal reports Copia Power, which develops, builds and operates grid-connected power and data center infrastructure, is working to rezone about 3,100 acres near Tonopah in the far West Valley for its latest project, the Belmont Energy Center. Most of the project site – about 2,860 acres – would be for utility-scale solar energy generation, while about 320 acres would be used for a gas generation facility, BESS and data centers. The project is backed by a $1.7 billion construction loan and has a power purchase agreement with APS. It’s expected to be operational within the next year. The post W. Valley Data Center Developer Building Massive Energy System appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Copia Power rezoning 3,100 acres near Tonopah, AZ (60 min west of Phoenix) for Belmont Energy Center.
Project: 2,860 acres solar, 320 acres gas/BESS/data centers; $1.7B construction loan, APS PPA.
Data center power constraints now require integrated renewable generation; operational in ~12 months.
stories.summary: Copia Power is rezoning 3,100 acres near Tonopah, Arizona (one hour west of Phoenix) for the Belmont Energy Center, combining 2,860 acres of utility-scale solar, 320 acres of gas generation, battery storage, and data centers. The project is backed by $1.7 billion in construction financing and a power purchase agreement with Arizona Public Service, with operations expected within the next year.
stories.impact: Data center proliferation in West Valley metro (driven by AI compute demand and Azure/AWS expansion in the Southwest) is creating a secondary demand wave for residential near Tonopah and broader Phoenix exurban markets. Developer teams should monitor Tonopah and surrounding unincorporated areas for inbound workforce demand; these tech-enabled energy hubs often precede multifamily need by 18–24 months, creating early-mover acquisition windows.

stories.title: Affinius Capital Lends $177M for Multifamily Asset Buy in New Jersey, Yonkers
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower and Waterfall Asset Management has sealed $177.25 million of acquisition financing for the purchase of two multifamily properties in the New York metropolitan area, Commercial Observer has learned. Affinus Capital provided the debt package for the sponsorship’s purchase of the 262-unit Edgewater Harbor property in Edgewater, N.J., and the soon-to-be completed 147-unit Trilogy Lofts at Tuckahoe project in Yonkers, N.Y. The deal involved a $124 million loan for Edgewater Harbor and $53.4 million of acquisition debt for Trilogy Lofts. The joint venture of Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower and Waterfall Asset Management acquired both properties from National Resources as part of a $450 million acquisition of four tri-state region properties encompassing more than 4 million square feet, CO previously first reported. “Edgewater and Trilogy Lofts represent a compelling opportunity to invest in high-quality, well-located multifamily assets in supply-constrained, transit-oriented submarkets with durable renter demand,” David Greenburg, managing director at Affinius Capital, said in a statement. “Waterfall Asset Management, Lincoln Property Company and Saber-Hightower bring institutional scale, local market expertise, and a proven track record of value-add execution that positions this portfolio for long-term performance.” Cushman & Wakefield negotiated the financing with a team consisting of John Alascio, Alex Hernandez, Brad Domenico, Chuck Kohaut and Mitch Rothstein. C&W also represented the seller in the acquisition with a Northeast capital markets team of Andy Merin, Frank DiTommaso and Ryan Dowd. Located at 45 River Road 6 miles from Midtown Manhattan, Edgewater Harbor features 60,500 square feet of retail space anchored by a Sprouts Farmers Market slated to open in 2027. bullets: Affinius Capital closed $177.25M acquisition debt for two tri-state multifamily properties via joint venture.
Edgewater Harbor (262 units, Edgewater NJ): $124M; Trilogy Lofts (147 units, Tuckahoe NY): $53.4M.

stories.summary: A joint venture of Lincoln Property Company, Saber-Hightower, and Waterfall Asset Management secured $177.25 million in acquisition financing from Affinius Capital for two multifamily assets: 262-unit Edgewater Harbor in Edgewater, New Jersey ($124M) and 147-unit Trilogy Lofts in Tuckahoe, New York ($53.4M). The financing is part of a $450 million portfolio acquisition of four tri-state properties totaling over 4 million square feet.
stories.impact: Active debt availability for core tri-state multifamily acquisitions signals lender appetite remains healthy despite office distress. However, the focus on transit-oriented, supply-constrained submarkets (Edgewater, Tuckahoe) indicates capital is concentrating in proven demand zones; development financing for secondary locations in NY metro remains difficult, compressing new supply in lower-barrier markets and supporting rent growth in constrained areas.

stories.title: Office CMBS Delinquencies Surpass September 2012’s All-Time High
stories.excerpt: The office CMBS delinquency rate rose to a new all-time high of 8.89% in July 2026, surpassing the previous peak of 8.83% recorded in September 2012 and up from 8.0% a year earlier, reported Fitch Ratings. Fitch’s overall U.S. CMBS delinquency rate increased 16 basis points to 3.49% in July from 3.33% in June, due primarily to new office delinquencies and the default of a large mixed-use portfolio SASB loan New 60+ day delinquency volume increased to $2.82 billion in July from $2.09 billion in June, led by office (40%, $1.12 billion), mixed-use (26%, $728 million), multifamily (14%, $405 million) and retail (10%, $274 million). Term defaults accounted for 67% ($1.88 billion) of new delinquencies, while maturity defaults represented 33%. Resolution volume declined to $1.54 billion in July from $1.63 billion in June. July resolutions included $785 million of loan liquidations, $677 million of loans brought current and $77 million of previously 60+ days delinquent loans removed from Fitch’s index after improving to 30 days delinquent. The post Office CMBS Delinquencies Surpass September 2012’s All-Time High appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Office CMBS delinquencies hit 8.89% in July 2026, surpassing Sept 2012 peak of 8.83%.
New 60+ day delinquencies: $2.82B in July; multifamily accounted for $405M (14% of total).
Overall CMBS delinquency rose to 3.49%; term defaults drove 67% of new delinquencies.
stories.summary: Office CMBS delinquencies reached an all-time high of 8.89% in July 2026, exceeding the previous peak from September 2012. New 60+ day delinquencies totaled $2.82 billion in July, with office accounting for 40% ($1.12B), mixed-use 26% ($728M), multifamily 14% ($405M), and retail 10% ($274M). The overall U.S. CMBS delinquency rate rose 16 basis points to 3.49%.
stories.impact: While office distress dominates headlines, multifamily delinquency uptick ($405M new 60+ day defaults) signals stress in value-add portfolios and refinancing pressure on 2021–2022 construction-loan cohorts. Developers with floating-rate bridge debt face maturity crunch; lenders are hardening underwriting and pushing longer rate-lock windows. Higher refinance spreads and stricter LTV/DSCR boxes will compress development feasibility across higher-cost metros (NY, SF, LA), particularly for non-trophy assets.

stories.title: Return to Lender: Week of August 20, 2026
stories.excerpt: Willow Grove Park Mall is set to be sold to a partnership of three New York firms, the Philadelphia Business Journal reported. Namdar Realty Group, Mason Asset Management and CH Capital Group are under contract to acquire the Montgomery County retail property. A representative for mall owner PREIT told the Business Journal that “a lender-directed sale process is underway and expected to be completed in the near term.” PREIT’s lender, PGIM Inc., listed the property’s debt for sale earlier this year after the Philadelphia company’s $170-million loan on Willow Grove Park Mall matured. Kingswood Center ($65.5 million | COMM 2018-COR3 | CMBX.12) liquidated this month via a discounted payoff, according to Morningstar Credit The resolution resulted in a $46.6-million loss on the loan. When factoring in non-recoverable advances, $53.7 million of losses hit the bonds, wiping out classes H-RR and G-RR and writing down F-RR by about 25%. The loan was backed by a 129,000-square-foot mixed-use building in Brooklyn. It was in special servicing since May 2023 after occupancy fell to 35%. Baltimore-based Atapco Properties has purchased Charlestowne North Apartments in Greenbelt, MD, a 178-unit affordable housing complex that has long faced serious financial and maintenance issues tied to its previous owner’s loan distress. The company bought the nine-story building for $22.6 million from Freddie Mac late last month, reported the Baltimore Business Journal. The price works out to roughly $126,000 a unit. The Pittsburgh Business Times reported that three office buildings totaling351,000 square feet at Parkway Center are scheduled to be auctioned off starting on August 24, according to a listing on TenX. The buildings are being sold at auction as part of a larger strategy by an investment sales team at JLL based in Pittsburgh and led by Mark Popovich. stories.title: PGIM Loans $83M to Refi 325-Unit New Jersey Apartment Complex
stories.excerpt: The final piece to a 1,300-unit apartment portfolio refinancing has been sealed. Commercial Observer can first report that Capodagli Property Company has secured $82.6 million to refinance Meridia Roselle Park 10, a 325-unit Class A multifamily complex in Roselle, N.J. PGIM provided the debt, structured as a bridge loan, while Greystone Capital Advisors’ Drew Fletcher, Bryan Grover, Miryam Reinitz-Kops and Jesse Kopecky arranged the transaction. The deal follows $287 million in cross-collateralized bridge financing PGIM had provided for four other Class A, multifamily assets in New Jersey throughout 2025. In total, PGIM provided $369.5 million in debt for a 1,340-unit multifamily portfolio comprised of Meridia Village Commons at 209 Valley Street in South Orange, N.J.; Meridia Pompton Lakes at 61 Wanaque Avenue in Pompton Lakes, N.J.; Meridia Linden 1001 at 1001 West Elizabeth Avenue in Linden, N.J.; and Meridia Little Ferry at 110 Bergen Turnpike in Little Ferry, N.J. Meridia Roselle Park 10 is at 10 West Westfield Avenue in Roselle Park, N.J., a suburb not far from Newark Liberty International Airport and 25 miles southwest of Times Square in Manhattan. Greystone’s Fletcher said in a statement that by breaking the cross-collateralized structure into separate deals, Capodagli Property Company was able to refinance each asset “on consistent terms as each came online,” giving each deal flexibility to seek out permanent financing at its own rate. “Completing this facility reflects the strength of our long-term relationship with Capodagli and PGIM’s continued conviction in their platform,” said Fletcher. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobsever.com.
bullets: PGIM refinanced 325-unit Meridia Roselle Park 10 (Roselle, NJ) with $82.6M bridge loan.
Part of 1,340-unit Meridia portfolio refi totaling $369.5M across five NJ multifamily assets.
PGIM provided $287M prior cross-collateralized bridge debt for four other Class A NJ assets in 2025.
stories.summary: Capodagli Property Company secured $82.6 million in bridge financing from PGIM to refinance Meridia Roselle Park 10, a 325-unit Class A complex in Roselle, New Jersey. The transaction completes a 1,340-unit portfolio refinancing, with PGIM having provided $369.5 million total debt across five New Jersey multifamily properties, following $287 million in cross-collateralized bridge financing in 2025.
stories.impact: Bridge lending remains available for stabilized, Class A multifamily portfolios in NJ; however, reliance on short-term debt signals owners are deferring permanent financing in hope of rate-cut tailwinds. When rates stabilize or hold, bridge maturities will force cap rate re-tests and potential distress. New development financing in NJ remains constrained; acquisition prices for stabilized assets will remain bid up by permanent-capital-constrained sponsors, crowding out ground-up development economics.

stories.title: Mamdani Wants to Add 18K New Homes on Staten Island
stories.excerpt: There’s a joke about how Staten Island got its name. Dutch settlers sailing into New York Harbor saw the 14-mile land mass and exclaimed “Is zat an island?” (You have to read it with the accent.) Is it the reality of how one of New York City boroughs got its name? No, but as the saying goes, “When the legend becomes fact, print the legend.” Fast forward to 2026, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has some big plans for the little island across the harbor from Manhattan. He is hoping to see a 9.5 percent growth in new homes on Staten Island over the next five years, or about 17,675 new homes across the borough, according to a growth plan from the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) released Wednesday. “As the city commits to ambitious housing action through the Block by Block plan, the draft Fair Housing Growth Strategy provides a framework for measuring need and understanding where we should grow, with fair housing at its center,” Sideya Sherman, director of the Department of City Planning, said in a statement. Staten Island is broken up in three segments: North Shore, Mid-Island and South Shore. The South Shore and Mid-Island are the island’s least dense areas. However, residents and elected officials on the South Shore have historically pushed back on more residential development in their neighborhoods, so the mayor could be facing an uphill battle. “Staten Island is probably the most perfect place in the world because you’re 20 or 40 minutes away from the largest city in the country, but at the same time it’s like being in New England,” Stuart Saft, a real estate lawyer with Holland & Knight, previously told Commercial Observer. “I’ve been to Staten Island, and it’s a magnificent place to be.” The mayor isn’t just targeting housing growth on Staten Island over the next five years, mind you. bullets: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani targets 17,675 new homes (9.5% growth) on Staten Island over five years.
HPD released Fair Housing Growth Strategy as part of Block by Block citywide housing plan.
Staten Island identified as key growth borough under revised zoning and housing policy.
stories.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled an ambitious housing growth plan for Staten Island, targeting 17,675 new homes (9.5% growth) over the next five years as part of the city's Block by Block initiative. The Department of Housing Preservation and Development released the Fair Housing Growth Strategy, positioning Staten Island as a key growth borough.
stories.impact: Staten Island zoning liberalization and explicit city housing targets signal major supply unlocking; developers should immediately acquire land and begin entitlement work on residential projects (especially transit-accessible sites near ferry terminals and planned transit upgrades). City backing ensures political runway and potential tax abatement/PILOT programs; the five-year timeline creates a narrow window before land costs reflect pent-up developer demand and density upside.

stories.title: Planet Fitness Takes 15K SF at Coney Island Residential Development
stories.excerpt: Wake up, it’s time for a workout. Planet Fitness has inked a 14,500-square-foot retail lease at the base of a new residential tower in Coney Island, Brooklyn, with Cammeby’s International Group and Rybak Development. Planet Fitness will move into the space at 532 Neptune Avenue next year on a 10-year lease with an asking rent of $65 per square foot, according to the New York Business Journal, which first reported the deal. Planet Fitness was represented by CBRE, while ownership was represented by Commercial Acquisitions. The names of the brokers on both sides of the deal were not immediately available. The brokerages did not immediately respond to Commercial Observer’s requests for comment. Planet Fitness has nearly 50 gyms in New York City across all five boroughs. The company did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. Cammeby’s and Rybak completed the three-tower, 499-unit residential complex at 532 Neptune late last year, featuring studio to three-bedroom homes. Some 30 percent of those units are designated as affordable housing. The development has 758,600 square feet of residential space, 40,368 square feet of ground-floor commercial space and 20,722 square feet of community facilities. The two developers aren’t stopping their work in Coney Island anytime soon, either, as Cammeby’s and Rybak submitted a rezoning application in March to build two 22-story residential buildings with a total of 703 units at 3030 Ocean Parkway and 400 Neptune Avenue. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Planet Fitness leased 14,500 SF at 532 Neptune Avenue (Coney Island, Brooklyn) on 10-year term.
Rent: $65/SF; developer Cammeby's/Rybak completed 499-unit mixed-use tower in late 2025.
30% of residential units are affordable; Planet Fitness moves in 2027.
stories.summary: Planet Fitness signed a 14,500-square-foot retail lease at 532 Neptune Avenue in Coney Island, Brooklyn, on a 10-year term at $65 per square foot. The space anchors a newly completed 499-unit residential tower developed by Cammeby's International Group and Rybak Development, with 30% affordable units. Planet Fitness will occupy the ground-floor retail beginning in 2027.
stories.impact: Grocery/fitness anchor tenancy at market-rate residential towers in outer-borough waterfront locations (Coney Island) validates mixed-use development model and supports absorption of new supply in historically lower-demand areas. Strong retail fundamentals suggest residential demand in Coney Island remains resilient; developers should prioritize similar mixed-use ground-floor activation in Kings County/Queens waterfront sites to unlock zoning density and support affordability mandates via market-rate rents and value capture.
